analysis.one_liner: Tightens SEC oversight of credit rating agencies and makes it easier to sue them for reckless ratings.
analysis.headline: The RATE Act, introduced in May 2009 to reform the credit rating agencies that misrated the securities behind the 2008 financial crisis, never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced credit rating agencies like Moody's, S&P, and Fitch to build internal controls for their ratings, manage and disclose conflicts of interest, disclose their fees from the companies they rate, and face lawsuits if they recklessly failed to verify the facts behind a rating. It grew out of the 2008 crisis, when these agencies stamped top grades on mortgage securities that later collapsed [S2, S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors: anyone with a pension, 401(k), mutual fund, or savings whose value depends on honest credit ratings. The bill's findings state that bad ratings of structured mortgage products contributed to the recent credit crisis and to mismanaged risk at financial institutions [S3]. Better oversight and easier lawsuits were aimed at preventing a repeat of that damage, which reached homeowners, retirement savers, and taxpayers who funded the bailouts.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the SEC to review each rating agency's internal controls, policies, and methodologies to make sure ratings follow the agency's own documented system [S3].

Requires agencies to adopt conflict-of-interest policies, directs the SEC to write rules on how agencies are paid by the companies they rate, and bans an agency from rating a structured product it previously advised on — addressing the issuer-pays conflict in which the company being rated also pays for the rating [S3].

Requires each rating agency to designate an independent compliance officer who reports on conflicts and cannot rate securities, sell services, or set pay for raters, and to file an annual public compliance report [S3].

Requires public disclosure of each agency's rating accuracy history so investors can compare agencies, and creates a standardized form explaining the assumptions, data limits, and weaknesses behind each rating [S3].

Lowers the legal bar for suing a rating agency: plaintiffs would only need to show a strong inference that the agency knowingly or recklessly failed to reasonably investigate or verify the facts its own methodology relied on [S3].
Requires a look-back review whenever an employee of a rated company had worked at the rating agency and participated in its ratings of that company within the past year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The credit rating agencies themselves, which would bear compliance costs, new SEC fines, disclosure duties, and expanded lawsuit exposure. Issuers and underwriters who buy ratings could also face higher fees if agencies passed costs on, and the bill's findings argue agencies should be held to the same liability standards as auditors and securities analysts [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the issuer-pays model in place: rather than changing who pays for ratings, it only directs a GAO study of alternative compensation arrangements, so the core conflict the bill targets would remain [S3].

Expanded private lawsuits against rating agencies could make agencies more cautious and litigation-averse, potentially raising the cost of ratings for all issuers, a cost that can be passed on to borrowers and investors.

Detailed SEC rulemaking over rating methodologies risks substituting regulator judgment for the agencies' own analytical judgment; the bill's own findings warn against regulators approving methodologies, while still directing the SEC to write rules on procedures and models [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, demonstrated failure — ratings that were inaccurate and influenced by conflicts helped cause the 2008 crisis, according to the bill's own findings [S3]. Its oversight, disclosure, and liability provisions were serious responses. Its biggest design weakness is that it regulated around the issuer-pays conflict rather than eliminating it, leaving the study of alternatives to a later report. The cost side — compliance, fines, and more lawsuits — falls almost entirely on a small, highly profitable industry that was receiving fees from the very companies whose products it rated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote, markup, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the RATE Act on May 19, 2009, during the period when Congress was examining the role of credit rating agencies in the financial crisis [S5].

The bill's findings state that ratings of structured financial products proved inaccurate in the recent credit crisis and contributed to mismanagement of risk by financial institutions and investors [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction; that referral is the last action recorded for the bill [S5].
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major credit rating agencies — Moody's, S&P, and Fitch — which kept their issuer-pays business model and high-fee structured rating business untouched by this bill, since it never advanced.

for.name: Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the RATE Act and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to Banking the same day [S5].

against.name: Chris Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the bill's referral was its last recorded action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only support shown in the record was the Democratic sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill would subject their ratings and pay structures to SEC review, require fee and conflict disclosures, ban rating structured products they pre-advised on, and lower the bar for lawsuits against them. Their interest in the bill ran against the public's, since their fees came from the issuers whose securities they rated and inflated ratings helped fuel the crisis [S3].
The bill requires written certification of due diligence services used in ratings, formalizing and expanding their role [S3].

industries.industry: Issuers and underwriters of structured securities
industries.note: They would face more scrutiny of the ratings they shop for and disclosure of the fees they pay agencies, raising the risk that inflated ratings become harder to obtain; their interest in easy, favorable ratings ran against investors' [S3].
